why: Floyd's algorithm, second phase: after slow and fast meet inside the cycle, a pointer restarted at the head and one left at the meeting point, both moving one step, meet exactly at the cycle entry. It takes fast/slow pointers plus the distance argument behind it.
hints: First, how do you know there is a cycle at all, and where can you get a point inside it in O(1) space?

Run fast/slow until they meet. If the head is a steps before the entry and they meet b steps into a cycle of length c, then 2(a + b) = a + b + kc, so a = kc - b: walking a steps from the meeting point lands on the entry.
After the meeting, set p = head, q = meeting node; advance both one step at a time until p == q; that node is the entry. Return -1 if fast reached the end.
pitfalls: If the head itself is in the cycle ("[0]" or "[1,0]"), the entry is node 0.
A set of visited nodes also works but uses O(n) space; the point here is O(1).
